stem: A 1-year-old boy has white hair, pale skin and blue-gray, translucent irises. He squints in bright light and has horizontal jerking eye movements. Both parents have dark skin. A skin biopsy shows a normal number of melanocytes that contain no melanin.
oneliner: 1-year-old boy + white hair, pale skin, translucent irises + photophobia, nystagmus + dark-skinned parents + normal melanocyte count without melanin → which complication is he at risk of?
ask: Which complication is he at greatest lifelong risk of?

options.B: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
options.C: Optic pathway glioma along the chiasm
options.D: Wilms tumor of the kidney in childhood

whyNot.A: Associated with **MEN2 and neurofibromatosis**; nothing here suggests a **catecholamine tumor**
whyNot.C: Seen in **neurofibromatosis type 1**; his findings are **hypopigmentation** with normal melanocyte number
whyNot.D: Linked to **WAGR and Beckwith-Wiedemann**; not to **lack of melanin**
whyNot.E: Follows **cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C or aflatoxin**; no liver risk here

answer: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
why: Pale skin, translucent irises, nystagmus and **melanocytes without melanin** is **oculocutaneous albinism** (**tyrosinase** defect, autosomal recessive). With no melanin to absorb **UV light**, he has a lifelong high risk of **skin cancers**, most often **squamous cell carcinoma**.
chain: Skin and eyes lack melanin protection from UV
UV damages keratinocyte DNA over years
Squamous cell carcinoma develops, plus basal cell and melanoma risk

idea.rule: Albinism is normal melanocytes with no melanin, so UV damage goes unchecked.
also: Ocular albinism: X-linked, eye findings only
Xeroderma pigmentosum: defective nucleotide excision repair with UV-induced skin cancers
Chediak-Higashi: partial albinism with recurrent infections

stem: A term newborn girl turns blue and dies of respiratory failure a few hours after birth. The pregnancy had almost no amniotic fluid from mid-gestation. She has a flattened nose, low-set ears and bilateral clubfeet, and autopsy shows absent kidneys, an intact diaphragm, and a normal trachea and esophagus.
oneliner: Term newborn girl + died of respiratory failure + almost no amniotic fluid + flat nose, low-set ears, clubfeet + absent kidneys, intact diaphragm → which lung abnormality?
ask: Which lung abnormality most likely caused her death?

whyNot.A: Hyaline membrane disease is a problem of **prematurity**; she was born at **term**
whyNot.C: Her **diaphragm is intact**, so abdominal organs did not compress the lung
whyNot.D: Her **trachea and esophagus are normal**, so there is no fistula
whyNot.E: This follows **weeks of ventilation and oxygen** in a premature infant; she died within hours

why: Absent kidneys mean no fetal urine, so there is almost **no amniotic fluid** (**Potter sequence**). Lung growth needs adequate fluid and fetal breathing movements, so the lungs stay small with too few alveoli. **Pulmonary hypoplasia** is the usual cause of death.

idea.rule: No amniotic fluid means small lungs: pulmonary hypoplasia.
also: Potter sequence: renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, flat face, limb deformities
Fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid in the second half of pregnancy
Posterior urethral valves can also cause oligohydramnios
Lung growth needs enough fluid and fetal breathing movements

chain: No kidneys, so no fetal urine
Almost no amniotic fluid after mid-gestation (oligohydramnios)
The fetus is compressed and lacks fluid for fetal breathing movements
The lungs stay small with too few airways and alveoli
Pulmonary hypoplasia causes respiratory failure soon after birth
